en: The First Section of the *Laghubhāgavatāmṛta*, titled *Śrī-Kṛṣṇāmṛta*: An Exposition on the Reality of the Blessed Lord, characterized by His self-manifested forms, His pastimes, and the manifestation of His own portions and expansions.
Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Obeisance to that Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa of unimpeded intelligence, who assumes countless portions of himself for the sake of the non-origination of all living beings. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.1.1)

The wise indeed worship Him who is dark-complexioned, yet black in splendor, together with His limbs, secondary limbs, weapons, and attendants, primarily through sacrifices consisting of congregational chanting. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.1.2)
May the flute-melody of Mukunda, swollen with the abundance of nectar flowing from his lotus-face, pour forth my bliss. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.1.3)
May those syllables "Hare Kṛṣṇa," uttered from the mouth of Śrī Caitanya, which immerse the world in divine love, be ever victorious; may they who call upon that name likewise triumph.
This very nectar of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, which was spread by the lotus feet of the venerable Prabhupāda,
is now being enjoyed in an abridged form.
This nectar, arising from its connection with Śrī Kṛṣṇa and His devotees, is twofold; first is the nectar of Kṛṣṇa, which is served here to His friends. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.1.6)
Relinquishing here my insistence on the elaboration of arguments,
sound alone is established as the authority regarding atoms because of its predominance.
Since they have demonstrated the principle that "the scripture is its source" (śāstrayonitvāt),
the supreme sages have accepted the authority of the Word alone.
Moreover, by the formulation of the principle "because reasoning is not firmly established" (tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt),
these very [scriptures] have made it perfectly clear that reasoning is not to be relied upon.
Now, in order to declare the preeminence among those worthy of worship by means of the abundance of his excellence, the various forms of Kṛṣṇa are described here in sequence. (Lbh 1.10)
Its own form is that which has a single essence with that [object], known as "possession" (āveśa);
thus it appears in three ways within the abodes that transcend phenomenal proliferation (prapañca). Lbh_1,1.11 //
In this context, "self-nature" (svayaṃrūpa) refers to that nature which does not depend on anything else; it is called self-nature.
Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Lord, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
he is Govinda, the beginningless beginning, the cause of all causes.
Thus (BrS 5.1),
here [it is said]: "having that as its single self-nature"—
that is, it shines forth by its own nature in non-difference from that which is its form.
Though appearing otherwise through forms and so forth, it is essentially of one nature with that [Self];
yet that manifestation again assumes two distinctions: as its own part and as its play.
In that regard, *vilāsa* (playful manifestation):
"That which appears as having another form than its own essential nature, generally through power (*śakti*) equal to itself—that is called *vilāsa*. (Lbh 1.15)
Just as Govinda is remembered as the Lord of the Supreme Ether (Paramavyoman),
so too is Vāsudeva the Lord of the Supreme Ether.

A "portion" (svāṃśa) is one of similar nature but with diminished power who manifests [the Lord]; he is called a portion, such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and others, or the Fish-incarnation and others, in their respective abodes. (Lbh 1.17)
In that regard, as for "possession" (āveśa):
those living beings who are possessed by Janārdana through a portion of his power of knowledge and so forth are called the "possessed ones" (āveśas), the most exalted of souls. (Lbh 1.1.18)
Just as Śeṣa, Nārada, Sanaka, and others [reside] even in Vaikuṇṭha,
these are likewise proclaimed in the tenth [chapter] by way of the example of Akrūra.
Thus there are three divisions; however, luminosity is not counted among the divisions, for it is not separate from them. (Lbh 1.20)
For instance:
when a single form is manifest in many places at once, that manifestation is said to be in every respect identical to its own nature. (Lbh 1.21)
"Just as Kṛṣṇa was manifest in every house in Dvāravatī—'How wonderful! and so forth—by such means of valid cognition he will be established. (Lbh 1.22)
Even when he has four arms in some instances, one should not abandon his nature as Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, this manifestation belongs to him even when he is two-armed.
The fact that these [deities] abide in a realm transcending conceptual proliferation is clearly manifest in various scriptures, such as the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma-purāṇa and others. (Lbh 1.24)
Thus concludes the first section: the exposition of the reality of the Lord, characterized by the manifestation of His own portions through the play of His own form.
**Second Chapter:
Exposition of the Incarnations as Persons and the Incarnations of Attributes**
Now the incarnations are described, in which Kṛṣṇa is most fully present.
The definition of that [incarnation] is as follows:

if those previously mentioned [deities], for the sake of the world's welfare, should manifest themselves as if unprecedented—either directly or through another medium—they are then known as incarnations (avatāras). (Lbh 1.2.2)
And that door is of the same nature as Him, and is indeed His devotee,
just as [the images of] Śeṣaśāyin and others, as well as Vasudeva and others, [are His devotees].
Those called "puruṣas" consist of the qualities (guṇas) and are playful in nature; they are of three kinds.
Generally, these [beings] are either partial incarnations (aṃśa), possessed incarnations (āveśa), or full incarnations (avatāra).
Among them, that which is the actual form itself will become manifest later.

In that regard, the characteristic of the Person (*puruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is as stated in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* (6.8.61): "He who, though one, experiences [the fruits of karma] in many ways according to his own qualities..."

Though pure, he appears as if impure through the distinctions of various forms; endowed with knowledge, the creator of the manifestations of all beings— to that eternal and imperishable Puruṣa, I bow forever.
Thus, [the master] says:
"Immediately after that very Supreme Lord, as stated in sequence. (Lbh 1.2.6)
Regarding this, the verse states:

"He who is a portion of the Supreme Lord, appearing as if possessing the qualities of primary matter (pradhāna), and whose activities consist of such acts as 'seeing' (īkṣā) and so forth—he is remembered as the Puruṣa, the manifold incarnation. (Lbh 1.2.7)
And its status as an incarnation is stated in the second book of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam:
"The first incarnation is the Supreme Person. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.2.8)
Thus (BhP 2.6.40),
and its divisions are as follows in the Sātvata-tantra:
The wise know that Viṣṇu indeed has three forms designated as Puruṣa:
the first is the creator of the Mahat; the second is situated within the threads [of the cosmic web]; and the third resides within all beings. By knowing these, one is liberated.
Thus [it is said]. (Lbh 1.2.9)
Regarding that, first:
as it is said in the eleventh [canto], Bhagavata Purāṇa 11.4.3— "When, by means of the five elements created by Himself..."
Having fashioned the city of Virāj,
the primordial god Nārāyaṇa entered it by means of a portion of himself and received the designation "Puruṣa."
And in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.10–13):
"Within that [liṅga], Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, became manifest."
Beginning with the verse "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads," that blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa emerged from that eternal one; as the essence of Saṅkarṣaṇa, he manifested from the ocean of causal waters.
While he was there, the great thousand-rayed sun himself fell into yogic sleep.
Within the network of the pores of his hair, the seed of Saṅkarṣaṇa produced golden eggs enveloped by the great elements.
This concludes [the section]. Lbh 1.2.11.
In this context, the mark (liṅga) is said to be a particularity of the limb of the self-nature (svayaṃ-rūpa).
The second [verse], which follows immediately after that same passage [BrS 5.14]:
"In this very way, one enters into each egg from a single part oneself. (Lbh_1.2.13)
Thus it is said in the Nārāyaṇopākhyāna of the Mokṣadharma: "He who lies in the waters of the womb, whose navel is a lotus, is this Aniruddha."
This very [state] is the regulator of Hiraṇyagarbha’s being Pradyumna.
Furthermore, that which would be the third form was also seen;
some [saw it] within their own bodies, according to the second verse of the second chapter.
Now, the descents of the qualities from that Puruṣa here are described:
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra, for the sake of the activities of maintenance, creation, and so forth. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.2.16)
As it was said in the first [chapter] (1.2.23):
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of Prakṛti; joined with these, the one Supreme Person assumes here the various forms of this [world]."
For the sake of maintenance and so forth, the names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara are applied;
indeed, among those, the qualities of goodness (sattva) lead to the highest welfare for men.
Thus [ends the section]. Lbh 1.2.17.
On this point, the verse states:
"Yoga is said to be a connection with the qualities by way of being their regulator;
therefore, it is not joined with them, because therein [yoga] is that which is its own part of the other. (Lbh 1.2.18)
In that regard, Brahmā—Hiraṇyagarbha—is subtle here, while the one known as Vairāja is gross;
he exists in two ways as the Lotus-born for the sake of experience and creation. (Laghu-bhārata 1.2.19)
Generally, it is Vairāja who, as the four-faced one, exists for the purpose of creation;
yet sometimes the Lord Viṣṇu himself, being Brahmā, creates.
And so it is stated in the *Pādma*:
"In some great aeon (*mahākalpa*), Brahmā may become a living soul (*jīva*) through his devotions; in another [aeon] here, Mahāviṣṇu attains the state of Brahmā. (Lbh_1,2.21)
Thus it is said.
In that great aeon (*mahā-kalpa*) wherein Viṣṇu assumes the role of creator, the Vairāja [being] enters him and enjoys the abundance of bliss;
therefore, the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) and the sovereignty of Brahmā exist according to the distinction of time. (Lbh 1.2.22)
In relation to his lordship, his status as an incarnation (avatāratā) is proclaimed in the scripture;

he is described as being close to the Blessed One by virtue of being a collective totality (samaṣṭi). His status as an incarnation is asserted by some as being through possession (āveśa), and by others in another way.
Likewise, in the *Brahma-saṃhitā* (5.49):
"Just as the sun manifests only a small portion of its own splendor within its own stones, so it is here."
I worship that Govinda, the primordial person, who is this Brahmā, the creator of the cosmic egg of the world. Lbh_1,2.24 //
Thus it is said:
"The birth of this one who dwells within the cosmic egg (garbhoda) from the navel-lotus is sometimes heard of; [his birth] also from water, fire, wind, and so forth. (Lbh 1.2.25)
Rudra is manifested in eleven forms, and likewise possesses eight bodies;
he is generally proclaimed to have five faces, three eyes, and ten arms.
In some places, a specific nature as a living being is attributed to Hara, just as it is to Brahmā;
let that [statement] remain merely as a residue (śeṣavat), since he is proclaimed to be a portion of Him.
Hara, because he is the abode of the Puruṣa, is essentially devoid of qualities;
yet here, due to his connection with Tamas, he is perceived by all as being subject to modification.
As it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.88.3):
"Śiva, eternally joined with Śakti, possesses three genders and is enveloped by the modes of nature."
Thus it is said; as in the Brahma-saṃhitā (5.45):
"Just as milk [becomes] curd through the application of a specific transformation..."
For that which is produced does not exist as something separate from its cause; I worship that Govinda, the primordial person, who likewise attains the state of Śambhu through his effects.
Thus [it is said]. Lbh 1.2.29.
At some time, his birth from the forehead of Brahmā, the Lord of Kamalā, may occur;
and at the end of the kalpa, he may even arise from Saṅkarṣaṇa as Kālāgni-rudra.
That form known as Sadāśiva is devoid of the scent of darkness;
it is the cause of all things and constitutes the very limbs of the Lord himself.
This same [form] is manifested in the world of Śiva within the regions of Vāyavya and the others.

And so it is said in the *Brahma-saṃhitā*, in the account of Ādi-Śiva (5.8): "That goddess Niyaṭi is Ramā; she is his beloved, and at that time she was under his control. His *liṅga* is the eternal Lord Śambhu, whose form is light."
"That which is the womb is the supreme power," and so forth.
Śrī Viṣṇu; as it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (3.8.16):
"Viṣṇu Himself entered that world-lotus, which was illuminated by all His transcendental qualities."
In him there came to be the Creator himself, composed of the Vedas, whom they call Svayambhū.
Thus [it is said]. Lbh 1.2.33.

That Viṣṇu who is recited is considered to be the one reclining upon the ocean of milk; because he is the playful manifestation (*vilāsa*) of Him who reclines within the cosmic egg (*garbhoda*), he is designated by the lords of sages as Nārāyaṇa, Virāṭ, and the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). (Lbh 1.2.34)
Those cities described in the Viṣṇudharmottara and other texts that exist within the interior of the cosmic egg, which are manifestations of Viṣṇu, shall now be recounted in brief. (Lbh 1.2.35)
For example:
"Above Rudra, at a distance of fifty thousand [yojanas], lies the world of Viṣṇu, which is proclaimed to be inaccessible to all worlds. (Lbh 1.2.36)
Above that is the Egg of Brahmā (brahmāṇḍa), endowed with a golden radiance.
To the east of Meru, in the middle of the salt ocean,
the great world of Viṣṇu is said to be situated within the waters.
There, in the waters of the Gharma, Janārdana, the god of gods, constantly sleeps together with Lakṣmī, reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa.
And in the eastern direction of Meru, in the midst of the Ocean of Milk,
there is another white city of the God situated in the middle of the milky waters.
There the Lord dwells, accompanied by Lakṣmī, seated upon the serpent Śeṣa;
there too he remains asleep for four months of the rainy season.
In that direction, in the midst of the Ocean of Milk,
there is an island twenty-five thousand yojanas in circumference,
renowned as Śvetadvīpa, most beautiful of all.
O Yādava, the men there possess the radiance of the sun, yet their appearance is like that of the cool-rayed moon; moreover, they are difficult even for the gods to behold because of their splendor.
And in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"There is a great island named Śveta, surrounded by the Ocean of Milk; it is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, most beautiful, and made entirely of gold. (Lbh_1,2.43)
Adorned with precious stones, he was washed on all sides by the ocean of milk, which possessed masses of restless waves resembling jasmine, the moon, and white water-lilies.
Thus it is said;
furthermore, it is proclaimed in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and other texts, as well as in the Mokṣadharma,
that there exists Śvetadvīpa on the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
To the north of Śuddhoda lies Śvetadvīpa, which is esteemed as equal to Padma.
Because Viṣṇu extends his being (*sattva*), he is remembered in the scriptures as *sattva-tanu* (one whose body is being).
Likewise, his multitude of incarnations (*avatāra*) is also *sattva-tanu*.
Or else, that [incarnation] is his "body" in the sense that it is an external locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*). (Lbh 1.2.47)
Therefore, the state of being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatā) is correctly established in all treatises.
For it is said in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.88.4):
"Hari is indeed devoid of material qualities, the direct Supreme Person beyond material nature;
He is the all-seeing witness. By worshiping Him, one becomes free from material qualities."
Thus [it is said]. Lbh 1.2.49.
"Therefore, it has been said: 'From this body of a sentient being, may there arise blessings.'"
Therefore, the scripture prescribes the very necessity of devotion to Him.
For it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Viṣṇu should be remembered constantly; he should never be forgotten.
All injunctions and prohibitions are but servants to these two. (Lbh 1.2.52)
Therefore, in that very same place (PadmaP 4.93.26):
"For the sake of deluding the world of moving and non-moving beings, let various ancient scriptures proclaim each respective deity as the supreme one until the end of the kalpa."
In the final conclusion, however, it is determined that there is only one Lord Viṣṇu, once all the operations of the scriptures have been subjected to analytical investigation.
In the first book (Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 1.2.26): Desiring liberation, those free from envy abandon the fierce-formed lords of beings and instead worship the peaceful portions of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus [ends the section]. Lbh 1.2.54.
In this context, the portions of Hari himself are designated by the word "kalā" (parts).
Therefore, the inferiority of all the gods, such as Brahmā, Indra, and the others, compared to Śrī Viṣṇu’s own classes of partial incarnations (aṃśa), has been clearly demonstrated.
As it is said in that very same place (1.18.21):
"Moreover, even this world, which has offered water of worship to Viriñca, was released by the water from the nails of his feet."
Furthermore, who else in this world besides Mukunda is worthy of the title "Lord" (Bhagavat), for he alone purifies all that remains?
Thus it is said; and in the Mahāvārāha-purāṇa: "The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, and the others are equal because of their non-difference from Viṣṇu."
Those beginning with Brahmā are said to be unequal; but primordial nature (prakṛti) is both equal and unequal.
Thus it is said.
In this context, by the word "prakṛti" (nature), the conscious power (*cic-chakti*) is denoted;
because it possesses both non-differentiated and differentiated forms, it is said to be both equal and unequal. (Lbh 1.2.59)
Thus concludes the examination of the descent of the Person (*puruṣāvatāra*) and the descent of the qualities (*guṇāvatāra*).
Chapter Three:
Examination of the Descent of Divine Play (*līlāvatāra*).
Now, the playful incarnations (līlāvatāras) are described according to my understanding, for the most part in accordance with the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata. (Lbh 1.3.1)
In that regard, the illustrious *Catuḥśataka* states in its first chapter (1.3.6):
"That very god Brahmā, having first resorted to the creation of the Kumāras, practiced the difficult-to-perform, unbroken vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). (Lbh_1,3.2)
Thus, this single descent is considered by the virtuous to be fourfold; because of the word "equal," it is remembered as the "Four Truths" (catuḥsatya) among those very four. (Lbh 1.3.3)
For the sake of propagating pure knowledge and devotion,
he descended from the lotus-born Brahmā as a fair-complexioned child of about five or six years of age.

Śrī Nārada: In that very place (1.3.8)—having attained the status of a celestial sage, he [Nārada] indeed described the third creation, that of the sages, because therein lies the Sātvata system, through which the state beyond action is achieved by means of action. (Lbh 1.3.5)
For the sake of setting this world in motion through his own devotion in every way,
Hari, as white as the moon, became the Creator in the form of a divine sage.
May these four Brahmās appear at the very beginning of the kalpa, and may Nārada and the others likewise persist throughout all kalpas. (Lbh 1.3.7)

Śrī-Varāha. In that very same place (1.3.7): "But for the sake of his [the world's] prosperity, the Lord of Sacrifice, intending to lift up the earth which had gone to the netherworld (rasātala), assumed a boar-like body. (Lbh 1.3.8)

And in the second [chapter] of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (2.7.1): "There, Ananta, having assumed the form of a Boar consisting of all sacrifices, rose up for the sake of uplifting the surface of the earth."
The wielder of the thunderbolt tore apart that primordial Daitya, who had come into the great ocean, as if splitting a mountain with his tusk.
Thus it was said:
"In this present kalpa, during the first interval of Manu Svāyambhuva, he appeared twice:
once from the nose of Brahmā for the purpose of lifting up the earth, and once from the water during the period of Cākṣuṣa. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.3.10)
To slay Hiraṇyākṣa during the lifting of the earth, this preeminent tusked one became the glorious four-legged Varāha; he is sometimes considered the "Boar among Men" (Nṛ-varāha). Lbh_1,3.11.
Sometimes dark as a rain-cloud, sometimes white as the moon,
this most ancient embodiment of sacrifice is remembered as being endowed with two colors.
The creation from Dakṣa Pracetasa is heard of in the Cākṣuṣa interval;
therefore, it is appropriate that the birth of Hiraṇyākṣa occurred at that very time. (Lbh 1.3.13)
For it is said in the glorious *Caturtha* [Purāṇa] (4.30.49):
"When the Cākṣuṣa interval had arrived and the previous creation had been swept away by Time, that Dakṣa, impelled by the gods, created the desired progeny. (Lbh 1.3.14)
Thus:
Diti was the daughter of Dakṣa, who was the son of the Pracetasas belonging to the lineage of Uttānapāda; Hiraṇyākṣa was the son of Diti. (Lalitavistara Bhāṣya 1.3.15)
At the beginning of the eon, there was no birth of a son even for Manu; where was that Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, where was Diti, and where was the son of Diti?
Therefore, Maitreya recounted the deeds of Śrī Varāha, which occurred across two different times, all together in one place, in accordance with the questions of Vidura.
It is stated in some Purāṇas that this dissolution occurred during the very interval of a Manu, due to a sage’s curse directed against that Manu. (Lbh 1.3.18)
This dissolution of Padmanābha, which occurred unexpectedly during the interval of the Manu Cākṣuṣa, is described in some places as being for the sake of his divine play (līlā).
"At the end of every manvantara, dissolution certainly occurs;
this was spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya in the Viṣṇudharmottara. (Lbh_1,3.20)
For it is thus:
when a *manvantara* has come to an end, the gods who were lords of that *manvantara*,
their defilements gone, reach the Maharloka and remain there.
And Manu, together with Śakra and the gods, O delighter of the Yadus,
attain the world of Brahmā, from which a return is difficult to obtain.
The earth, the seven underworlds, and Maheśvara in the form of water—possessing garlands of waves and great velocity—stand encompassing everything. (Lalitavistara 1.3.23)
O Yādava, O Indra among kings, everything resting upon the Bhūrloka perishes at that time, yet the renowned mountain ranges of the world do not perish. (Lbh_1,3.24)
Then, O scion of the Yadu clan, the goddess Earth became a boat and supported all seeds without exception.
And there will be future Manus and likewise future ṛṣis;
they, O tiger among kings, remain there as those seven renowned upon the earth.
Assuming the form of a fish, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World,
became a horned creature and effortlessly drew that boat from place to place.
Having moored his boat upon a peak of the Himālaya mountains, the Lord of the World, in the form of a fish, becomes invisible; and those who were there remain in that place.

O lord of men, for as long as it takes to perform an act equal to that which has been done, the waters are said to be cleansed; they then return to their former state of tranquility, and at that time, both the sages and Manu perform everything just as before. (Lalitavistara 1.3.29)
Thus: "There is no dissolution at the end of Manu; it was shown to Manu by Viṣṇu through his illusory power (māyā). Those who speak thus do not consider this [teaching] to be their own. (Lbh 1.3.30)
In the first book of the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (1.3.15): "During the deluge of the ocean at the end of Cākṣuṣa Manu’s era, He assumed the form of a fish;
having placed the earth upon a boat, He protected Vaivasvata Manu. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.3.31)
And in the Śrī-dvitīya (2.7.22): "At the time of the end of the Yuga, a fish consisting of the earth, the abode of all multitudes of living beings, was found by Manu."
Having seized my heads— which had fallen into the water during that great terror— he sported there with them, cutting away the paths of the Vedas.
And in the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"Thus addressed by Brahmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, the Supreme Lord, assumed the form of a fish and entered the great ocean. (Lbh_1,3.33)
In this kalpa, Matsya also appeared twice, like Varāha;
at the beginning of the Svāyambhuva period, he slew the Daitya and recovered the Vedas,
while at the end of the Cākṣuṣa period, he bestowed his grace upon Satyavrata.
The conduct of the first [Tathāgata] was proclaimed by the final half-verse, and that of the last by the preceding half-verse; he is to be known as a fish, like the Boar.
This is merely an illustration; the fourteen manifestations of other Manvantaras are to be known from the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī-Yajña,

having attained the status of a king of men (nara-devatva) with the desire to accomplish the work of the gods, performed heroic deeds thereafter, beginning with the subduing of the ocean. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.3.37)
Thus,
because he removes the great suffering of the three worlds,
he was also designated as "Hari" by his maternal grandfather, Manu.
Śrī Nara and Nārāyaṇa were right there (1.3.9):
"In the fourth creation, that of the portion of Dharma, the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, having come into being, performed difficult penance endowed with self-serenity. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.3.39)
Thus,
in the scripture, two others named Hari and Kṛṣṇa are recorded as their uterine brothers;
by these four together, there would be a single incarnation, just as in the case of Sanaka and the others.

Śrī Kapila, in that very same place (1.3.10)— the fifth [incarnation] named Kapila, the Lord of Siddhas, taught the Sāṅkhya system, which determines the collection of principles, to Āsuri, as it had been corrupted by time. (Lbh 1.3.41)
Thus,
having manifested from Kardama through Devahūti, he was given the name Kapila by Viriñci because of his tawny (kapila) complexion. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.3.42)
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*:
"Kapila, who is a portion of Vāsudeva, proclaimed the Sāṅkhya doctrine to the gods beginning with Brahmā, and likewise to Bhṛgu and the others."
In the same way, it was augmented by all the meanings of the Vedas for the sake of the Asuras.
And Kapila, as well as others, proclaimed the Sāṅkhya system—which is contrary to all the Vedas, which was taught to Āsuri, and which is bolstered by fallacious reasoning. (Lbh 1.3.44)
Śrī-dattaḥ / Regarding Śrī-dvitīya (2.7.4): He who is the descendant of Atri, whom the Lord— being pleased with one who desired offspring— said, "I am given by me," he is Datta.
Those whose bodies were purified by the dust of his lotus feet— the Yadus, Haihayas, and others— attained both kinds of yogic perfection.
And in the first [chapter] of the Śrī [Bhāgavata] (1.3.11):
"The sixth [son], Atri, was chosen and obtained as a son by Anasūyā;
he taught Ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda, and others. (Lbh 1.3.46)
In the Śrī-Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, however, it is told that the Blessed One, being entreated by Anasūyā, the wife of Atri, entered into the state of being Atri’s offspring.
For instance:
Having granted a boon to Anasūyā, Viṣṇu, who pervades the entire universe,
became the son of Atri through her, assuming a human form by his own will.
Known as Dattātreya, he was adorned with the garb of an ascetic.
In the *Śrī-Hayaśīrṣā*, the second [part] (2.7.11):
"In that sacrificial session, the Blessed Lord Hayaśīrṣa was present for me."
He was the manifest Person of Sacrifice, golden-hued, composed of the Vedic meters, consisting of the sacrifice, and the self of all the deities;
from his nostrils as he breathed, there issued forth the longing words of the Vedas.
Thus,
having manifested from the sacrificial fire and slain the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the Lord of Vāgīśvarī brought back the Vedas once again.
Śrī-Haṃsa said: "O Śrī-Dvitīya (2.7.19)—
to you and to Nārada, the Blessed Lord, being greatly pleased by his increased devotion, spoke well of yoga."
And they who have taken refuge in Vāsudeva know directly that Vaiṣṇava knowledge which is the lamp illuminating the true nature of the self. (Lbh 1.3.51)
"Thus am I capable of discerning everything, like the separation of milk from water"— manifesting this, the royal swan has emerged from the water. (Lbh 1.3.52)
The beloved of Śrī Dhruva; in that very place (2.7.8):
"Though but a child, pierced by the arrows discharged by his co-wife in the presence of the king, he went to the forests for asceticism."
Therefore, being pleased, he granted the state of stability to the one who praised him;
for the divine sages praise that which is above and below.
Thus,
because an incarnation is mentioned in the *Svāyambhuva* [Purāṇa] while the name is not stated,
and because sacrifices and other rites are mentioned there, [the subject here is determined] by the means of proof known as "presumption by elimination" (*pāriśeṣya*).
By virtue of renown, he is called by that name "Pṛśnigarbha," just as in the verse beginning with "O, this is the mountain! [the mountain] is referred to as "Govardhana Mountain. (Lbh 1.3.54)
Likewise, in the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (10.3.32):
"In a previous creation, during the time of Svāyambhuva Manu, you yourself were Pṛśni;
at that time, this Prajāpati named Sutapā was free from all blemish."
"I became your son, known as Pṛśnigarbha."
Thus,
because their conduct is not mentioned here and their names are not mentioned there,
and because they are mutually dependent, their connection in a single place is indeed logical.
If the status of being an incarnation were established merely by coming here,
then it would follow that this could be postulated at will in other places as well.
Śrī-Ṛṣabha;
Śrī-Prathama (1.3.13):
"In the eighth [manvantara], Urukrama was born from Nābhi by Merudevī."
Showing the path of the wise, which is honored by all stages of life.
Śukla is capable of making known the dharma of the supreme *paramahaṃsas*;
he is manifest through his excellent qualities and is renowned by the name Ṛṣabha. (Lbh 1.3.59)

Śrī-Pṛthu: In that very context (1.3.14)—Requested by the sages, he assumed a ninth earthly form; O brahmins, he milked the medicinal herbs from this earth, and for that reason, he is the most beloved. (Lbh 1.3.60)
Thus,
O Great King, from the left arm of the sage Viṣṇu, who was being churned by the hosts of sages,
Pṛthu appeared, possessing the luster of pure gold.
In the first [Manvantara], thirteen [beings] beginning with Kumāra and ending with Pṛthu were manifest;
however, Kela and Amatsya attained manifestation again during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.

Now, regarding Śrī-Nṛsiṃha: in that very same place (1.3.18)—assuming his fourteenth form as Nārasiṃha, he tore apart the powerful lord of the Daityas with his claws upon his lap, just as a mat-maker tears apart a reed-mat. (Lbh 1.3.64)
In the sixth interval, prior to the churning of the ocean by Nṛhari, he had previously existed;
therefore, before that, he manifested as the Tortoise and other forms during the sixth interval.

Śrī-Kūrma: In that very place (1.3.16)—"While the gods and asuras were churning the ocean with Mount Mandara as the churning-stick, the omnipresent Lord assumed the form of a tortoise and supported it upon his back in his eleventh incarnation. (Lbh 1.3.66)

Thus it is said in the *Pādma*: "Requested by the gods, he assumed this very form consisting of earth. But in another scripture, it is stated that at the beginning of the kalpa, the Supporter of the Earth became manifest.

Śrī-Dhanvantari and Mohinī: In that very place (1.3.17)—"He caused the other gods to drink the twelfth [nectar], that of Dhanvantari, and the thirteenth as well, while bewildering them with the woman Mohinī. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.3.68).
Thus it is said.
Regarding this, the illustrious Dhanvantari states:
"And in the sixth and seventh [kalpas], he has appeared twice. (Laghu-bhārata 1.3.69)
In the sixth interval, after the churning of the ocean, he emerged with two arms, dark-complexioned, holding a water-pot filled with nectar, and was the promulgator of Āyurveda;
and in the seventh [interval], being of such a form, he became the son of the King of Kāśī.
Śrī Mohinī:
For the purpose of enchanting the Daityas and for the delight of Dhūrjaṭi, the Unconquered One has appeared twice in the form of Mohinī. (Lbh 1.3.71)
Thus, in this sixth [chapter], four forms of Nṛsiṃha have been proclaimed.

Śrī-Vāmana: In that very place (1.3.19)—having assumed the form of Vāmana, he entered the sacrifice of Bali, requesting three paces while desiring to reclaim the triple heaven. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.3.73)
Thus,
Vāmana, having manifested himself three times in this kalpa,
first went to the sacrifice of Vāsaki, the lord of the Dānavas.
Then, in this Vaivasvata Manvantara, during the seventh Caturyuga of this [cycle], he went to the sacrifice of Dhundhu; born to Aditi from Kaśyapa,
there were born exactly three Trivikramas for the sake of receiving gifts.

Śrī-Bhārgava: In that very place (1.3.20)—observing the kings who were enemies of Brahman during his sixteenth incarnation, he became enraged and twenty-one times made the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas. (Lbh 1,3.75)
Thus it is said:
"Some say that Gaura attained manifestation from Reṇukā and Jamadagni in the seventeenth [cycle] of the four-yuga era, while others say it was in the twenty-second. (Lbh 1.3.76)
Śrī Rāghavendra states in that very same work (1.3.22):
"Having attained the state of a god among men out of a desire to accomplish the work of the gods, he thereafter performed heroic deeds such as the subduing of the ocean. (Lbh 1.3.77)
Thus,
in the twenty-fourth cycle of four ages, during the Tretā Yuga, he appeared in Kauśalyā from Daśaratha, possessing the luster of a fresh blade of dūrvā grass.
Accompanied by Bharata and the two sons of Sumitrā.
In this scripture, these three manifestations beginning with Lakṣmaṇa are recorded:
here Bharata is dark as a rain cloud, while the two sons of Sumitrā possess a golden luster.
In the Padma [Kalpa], Bharata and Śatrughna are proclaimed as the conch and the discus;
and there, Śrī Lakṣmaṇa is designated as Śeṣa.
Śrī Vyāsa: In that very same place (1.3.21):
"Then, born from Parāśara upon Satyavatī as the seventeenth [generation], he saw that men possessed little intelligence and thus composed the branches of the Vedic tree. (Lbh 1.3.81)
Because Śauri (Kṛṣṇa) said, "I am Dvaipāyana among the Vyāsas," he is therefore described specifically in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and other such works. (Lbh_1.3.82)
As it is said: "Know Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana Vyāsa to be Nārāyaṇa himself;
for who else but the Lotus-Eyed One could be the author of the Mahābhārata?"
Thus [it is said]. Lbh 1.3.83.
It is heard that Apāntaratamas entered Dvaipāyana;
did he attain union (*sāyujya*) with him here, or might he even be a portion (*aṃśa*) of Viṣṇu?
Therefore, some say that this was merely an "entrance" (*āveśa*). (Lbh 1.3.84)
Now, regarding Śrī Rāma and Kṛṣṇa:
in the first [chapter], verse 1.3.23— having attained birth among the Vṛṣṇis in the nineteenth and twentieth [incarnations].
As Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, the Blessed One removed the burden of the earth.
Thus said Śrī Rāma:
"He has manifested from Janaka and Vasudeva through his two mothers."
He who always has a complexion like that of fresh, solid sandalwood and wears garments dark blue as a rain cloud; Lbh_1,3.86.
The second manifestation is Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is indeed Rāma;
having united with Śeṣa, the upholder of the earth, he has attained manifestation. (Lbh 1.3.87)
The remainder [of the devotees] of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow is twofold: those who support the earth and those whose form is the bed.
Among them, due to the penetration (āveśa) of Saṅkarṣaṇa, the supporter of the earth is considered Saṅkarṣaṇa himself;
likewise, the one whose form is the bed possesses the conceit of friendship and servitude toward Him.
Śrī-Kṛṣṇa:
He has manifested in his mother Devakī from his father Ānaka-dundubhi; though dark as a rain-cloud and two-armed, he is also four-armed.
The Glorious Buddha. In that very place (1.3.24):
"Then, when the Kali age has begun, for the purpose of deluding the enemies of the gods, one named Buddha, the son of Añjana, will appear among the Kīkaṭas. (Lalitavistara 1.3.90)
Thus it is said:
"When two thousand years of the Kali age have passed, he will appear manifest with a pale-red complexion, having two arms and hairless. (Lbh 1.3.91)
When the charioteer told the story, the Buddha’s realization was brought to mind:
"This very event has now occurred in the Forest of Dharma that has arisen."
Śrī-Kalki: In that very same place (1.3.25)—"Then, at the junction of the ages, when kings consist mostly of robbers, the Lord of the World, Kalki by name, will be born from Viṣṇuyaśas. (Lbh 1.3.93)
Thus it is proclaimed in the Padma Purāṇa: "In the past, he was Manu, Daśaratha, and Vasudeva; and in the future, he will be Viṣṇuyaśas. (Lbh 1.3.94)
The sovereignty of that Kalkin has been well described within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). By some it is proclaimed that in every Kali age there shall be a Buddha, and he shall be Kalkin.
These eight, beginning with Vāmana, are said to belong to the Vaivasvata [Manvantara].
These twenty-five are called the "descents into the aeons" (kalpāvatāra),
because they generally appear once during each aeon.
Thus concludes the description of the playful incarnations (*līlāvatāra*).
Chapter Four: Now, the incarnations during the periods of the Manvantaras (*manvantarāvatāra*).
This incarnation during the Manvantara was primarily for the sake of slaying the enemy of Śakra;
it was the manifestation of Mukunda among the gods as his ally. (Lbh 1.4.1)

When the state of descending into the eons (*kalpa*) is established, it is also clear that sacrifices and other rites descend during the intermediate periods of Manu (*manvantara*), because they are maintained until the end of each such period. (Lbh 1.4.2)
In the Manvantaras beginning with that of Svāyambhuva, these incarnations, starting with Yajña and ending with Bṛhadbhānu, are considered to appear in successive order. (Lbh 1.4.3)
Regarding the sacrifice in the first [age], that of Svāyambhuva:
since the sacrifice has already been explained previously, it is not recorded here.
As it is said in the eighth chapter (8.1.21–22):
"The seer Vedaśiras had a wife named Tuṣitā;
from her was born the god renowned as Vibhu. (Lbh 1.4.5)
Eighty-eight thousand sages who maintained their vows followed his vow, for he was a celibate from his youth.
Thus it is said.
In the third [chapter], the *Auttamīya*, Satyasena states: "But the Blessed One, Puruṣottama, [was born] from Dharma and Sūnṛtā. (8.1.25–26)
He was born together with those who were devoted to truth, renowned as Satyasena.
Accompanied by Satyajit, he struck down the untruthful, vow-breaking, and ill-behaved Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, as well as the malevolent spirits and hosts of elemental beings.
Thus [it is said].
In the fourth [incarnation], Hari was born of Tāmasī; there also, the Blessed Lord Hari was born from Harimedhas through Hariṇī.
By whom [the name] "Hari" was invoked, by him Gajendra was liberated from the crocodile.

Thus it is remembered: those devoted to right conduct should always remember Hari, the liberator of the lord of elephants, every morning for the destruction of all that is undesirable. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.4.10)

In the fifth [manvantara], Raivatya, Vaikuṇṭha [appeared]—Vikuṇṭhā was the wife of Śubhra; from them, by their own portions and through the Vaikuṇṭhas, the best of gods, the Lord Vaikuṇṭha himself was born. (Lbh 1.4.11)
By him, who desired to please his beloved, Vaikuṇṭha was fashioned as a world honored by the worlds, at the request of the goddess Ramā. (Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta 1.4.12)
Thus:
"The manifestation of the pervasive and immutable Mahā-Vaiṣṇava realm upon the foundation of truth is called *kalpanā*. (Lbh 1.4.13)
And in the sixth [Manvantara], that of Cākṣuṣa, O Ajita, there too, in Devasambhūti, there was a son of Vairāja,
the Lord named Ajita, the master of the world, who appeared by means of a portion [of the Divine]. (Lbh_1,4.14)
By whom, having churned the ocean, the nectar was secured for the gods;
and who, wandering in the waters, supported Mount Mandara in the form of a tortoise. (Lalitavistara 1.4.15)
Thus, in the seventh [manvantara], the Vaivasvata, Vāmana says:
"In the Vaivasvata interval, that Vāmana has already been manifested, as previously stated."
Seven future [Manus] are spoken of as being in the Sāvarṇya intervals and so forth.
In the eighth Manvantara, according to the Sāvarṇika [account], there will be a sovereign ruler (Sārvabhauma):
"From Devaguha, on the Sarasvatī, the powerful lord named Sārvabhauma shall take the position from Purandara and bestow it upon Bali" (BhP 8.13.17). Lbh_1.4.17.
Thus, in the ninth [manvantara], that of Dakṣasāvarṇi, there was Ṛṣabha (8.13.20):
"To the long-lived one, in Ambudhārā, Ṛṣabha was a portion of the Blessed One."
By which he will become one who enjoys the three worlds when they have been brought to perfection—a marvelous being.
Thus,
in the tenth [manvantara], the Brahma-Sāvarṇika, Viṣvaksena (8.13.23)—
Viṣvaksena will indeed establish friendship with Śambhu in the Viṣūcī [kalpa].
The all-pervading Lord, the creator of the universe, was born by his own portion in the house of Viśvasṛj.
Thus, in the eleventh [chapter], the *Dharmasāvarṇanīya*, it is stated regarding Dharmasetu (8.13.26):
"The son of Āryaka is there remembered as Dharmasetu."
During the Vaidhṛta yoga, a portion of Hari will uphold the three worlds.
Thus it is said:
in the twelfth Manvantara, that of Rudrasāvarṇi, he who is called Sudhāmā—an expansion (*aṃśa*) of Hari—will bring about the success of that Manu's purpose. (8.13.29)
The son of Truth and Might, the pervasive one, born of Sunṛtā.
In the thirteenth Manvantara, that of Devasāvarṇi, Yogeśvara— (8.13.32)—
the son of Devahotra, the offerer of oblations to the Lord of Heaven,
Yogeśvara, an expansion of Hari, will be born of Bṛhatī. (Lbh_1,4.22)
Thus, in the fourteenth [manvantara] of Indra-Sāvarṇi, Bṛhadbhānu [is mentioned] at 8.13.35:
"Then Hari was Bṛhadbhānu, the son of Satrāyaṇa."
O Great King, in this canopy, the threads of activity have been stretched out.
Since the two [incarnations] as Yajña and Vāmana are already mentioned there [in the previous list],
twelve incarnations during the Manvantaras are stated in this enumeration.
Thus concludes the description of the incarnations during the Manvantaras.
Now, the incarnations during the Yugas are described: in the Satya-yuga, Hari is white by name and complexion.
He was red in the Kṛta age, dark in Tretā, black in Dvāpara, and [dark] in Kali. (Lalitavistara 1.4.25)
For the sake of specific modes of worship during the ages such as the Satya-yuga and others,
he likewise descends in succession as the Manvantara-avatāra.
These forty-one incarnations, which bring about the manifestation of kalpas, manvantaras, and yugas, have thus been declared.
The Brahma-kalpas and others, ending with the Pādma-kalpa, have occurred by the thousands;
this present kalpa is called Śveta-vārāha.
Those who appeared at the beginning of the Brahma-kalpa during the Svāyambhuva interval,
as well as Kumāra, Nārada, and others, were manifest in the subsequent intervals such as that of Cākṣuṣa.
Generally, in each kalpa there arise these beings known as Svāyambhuva and so forth;
they are the Manus, as well as the incarnations and those named after sacrifices and the like. (Lbh 1.4.30)
For thus it is stated in the Śrī-Viṣṇudharmottara, in the inquiry of Śrī Rudra:
"O twice-born one, these fourteen Manus who have been described by you are indeed [the presiding deities] when the eternal day of Brahmā has arrived, occurring in their respective order."
Or are there others as well, O Knower of Dharma? Cut through this doubt of mine.
From the *Śrī-Mārkaṇḍeyottara*:
"O Great King, these very fourteen Manus are to be known by you in every kalpa; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter."
Indeed, all of them must be understood by you as being of one form;
yet some appear slightly different due to the illusory power (māyā) of the Supreme Lord.

Thus, there are four types of descents (*avatāra*): those of possession (*āveśa*), those of power (*prābhava*), as well as states of majesty (*vaibhava*) and supreme states (*parāvasthā*). (Lbh 1.4.34)
In that regard, the descents through possession are to be understood according to the method previously described,
such as those of Kumāra, the divine sages, Veṇāṅga, Prabhāva, and others.
As it is stated in the *Pādma*:
"The omnipresent Lord Hari entered into the Kumāras and into Nārada. (Lbh 1.4.36)
As it is said in that very same place:
"The four-armed God, bearing the conch and the discus, entered into Pṛthu. (Lbh 1.4.37)
And it is proclaimed in that very same place that he became possessed by Bhārgava.
For thus it has been told to you, O Goddess, the life-story of the high-souled Jamadagni,
the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow, concerning his descent through the penetration of Śakti.
Thus,
the state of being an incarnation of Kalkin is also observed in the Viṣṇudharma.
Just as the Lord Hari is not seen in the Kali age bearing a perceptible form as he was in the Kṛta and other ages, for that very reason he is proclaimed to have three ages (tri-yuga).
And when the end of the Kali age has arrived, Vāsudeva, having entered into Kalki, the expounder of the Veda, establishes the stability of the world.
In the Kali age, the Lord enters into those various previously arisen beings and performs whatever he intends for himself.
Thus,
therefore, the superiority among these would be merely figurative.

Now, those who possess the power of sovereignty and whose forms are of the nature of Hari, yet are inferior to those in the supreme state, receive various designations according to the gradation of their powers in successive order. (Lbh 1.4.45)
And therein, through the eye of the scriptures, two kinds of powerful beings are seen:
some whose manifestation has not been very long and whose fame is not very extensive;
they are Mohinī, Haṃsa, Śukla, and others who follow the cycles of the ages.
Other authors of treatises were mostly those who acted like sages;
they were Dhanvantari, Ṛṣabha, Vyāsa, Datta, and Kapila.
Now, there may be states of manifestation: he is Kūrma, the lord of sages;
Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara; Śrīvarāha, and Hayānana.
Pṛśnigarbha, Pralambaghna, and the fourteen beginning with Yajña—
these twenty-one are declared to be the states of manifestation (vaibhavāvasthā).
Those two, Kroḍa and Hayagrīva, arise within the ninefold manifestation (navavyūha);
likewise, there are four preeminent ones during the incarnations in the Manvantaras.
Śrī, Hari, Vaikuṇṭha, as well as Ajita and Vāmana—
these six are considered the states of manifestation (vaibhavāvasthā), which are regarded as being comparable to the supreme state (parāvasthā).
The locations of some of these, which shine here and there within the center of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), are recorded according to the perspective of the scriptures;
in this regard, the statements of the Viṣṇudharmottara and other such texts are accepted as authoritative. (Lbh_1,4.52)
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Above that is another [world] of the same extent;
it is renowned as Mahātala, and the fifth has a red ground."
There shall be a lake measuring one hundred thousand yojanas,
and Hari himself dwells there, assuming the form of a tortoise.
Above that,
at the same distance in extent, there is a divine lake measuring three hundred yojanas;
in it dwells the god Hari, assuming the form of a fish.
Nārāyaṇa, the friend of men, dwells at the site of the Badarī tree.
The abode of the Man-Lion is proclaimed to be in Maharloka,
measuring three hundred thousand yojanas in extent.
And fifty thousand [leagues], the remaining portion is enchanting.
That very world was described as the Self-luminous Boar;
this world, attached to the cosmic egg, is situated at the very bottom and is enchanting.
There the Blessed One, in the form of a boar, dwelt, assuming a white-colored body.
Above that, of the same extent in measurement,
is the fourth yellow earth known as Gabhastitala;
there dwells the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the god who bears the horse-head.
Resembling a hundred moons, he was adorned with ornaments of gold.
The abode of Pṛśnigarbha, the Brahman, is above the world.
The garment of the enemy of Prahamba should be placed in that very place where the garment of the enemy of Agha is located.
He himself, a portion of this very [deity], dwells in Pātāla,
eternally bearing the palm-tree banner, eloquent, and adorned with a forest garland.
Constantly bearing upon his head a hooded canopy variegated with jewels,
he carries a plow, a mace, and a sword, adorned with dark blue garments.
And above the world of Brahmā, the world of Hari shines resplendently.
The abode of the high-souled Viṣṇu Vaikuṇṭha is in the heavenly world (svarloka),
as well as in the world of Vaikuṇṭha itself, where he has manifested in person.
The residence of Ajita is established in the Dhruvaloka,
while the dwelling of the great-souled Vāmana is in the Bhuvarloka.
The abode of Trivikrama is proclaimed to be in the world of asceticism (tapas);
likewise, his divine refuge in Nārāyaṇa is situated in the world of Brahmā;
and above the world of Brahmā, a dwelling was constructed by him.
That which was told by Surendra to the celestial rishi in the Hari-vaṃśa;

For it is said in the *Harivaṃśa* (2.70.37): "O Blessed One, O Sage, having consumed this great earth which was fashioned by Viṣṇu, [he established] a world superior to all the worlds above. (Lbh_1,4.68)
Thus [it is said].
It is established in the treatise that the most wonderful abodes of all the incarnations shine forth in the supreme realm. (Lbh 1.4.69)
For it is said in the Padma-purāṇa:
"In the eternal realm of Vaikuṇṭha, all the most radiant incarnations, such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and others, always reside there. (Lbh_1,4.70)
Thus concludes the fifth chapter: the determination of the descent [of the teaching] and its location,
and the determination of the supreme state.
Then, in some places he was called "the incarnation of Nara's brother," and in others "Upendra"; thus, that brother was not very well-known.
As it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The two sons of Dharma, known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who were portions (aṃśa) of Hari, entered the Lunar dynasty and were born as both Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna. (Lbh 1,5.2)
